name: Clark Clifford

summary.text: Clark M. Clifford was a Washington lawyer and former U.S. Secretary of Defense who served as chairman of First American Bankshares, the Washington bank holding company that the Federal Reserve and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee found had been secretly controlled by BCCI. He and his law partner Robert Altman also acted as counsel to BCCI. Both were indicted by federal and New York grand juries in July 1992; the New York case against Clifford was dismissed in November 1993 on the ground that he was not fit to stand trial, and Altman was acquitted by a New York jury in August 1993. In February 1998 Clifford and Altman settled the Federal Reserve Board's administrative proceedings against them without admitting the Board's allegations.

facts.claim: Clark Clifford was chairman of First American Bankshares and Robert Altman its president. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) states that Clifford and Altman created a shell corporation, in the form of a trust, to hold the Financial General Bankshares stock, and that Clifford was in effect a trustee because Altman held a power of attorney for virtually every shareholder. The Federal Reserve Board stated in 1998 that both men had served as directors of Credit and Commerce American Holdings, N.V., formerly a bank holding company, and of its subsidiary First American Bankshares, and that both had acted as counsel to BCCI.
facts.quote: Clifford, who became Chairman of First American was essentially a trustee since his associate, Robert Altman, the President of First American, held a power of attorney for virtually every shareholder.

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) found that, regardless of whether Clifford and Altman were deceived by BCCI in some respects, both men participated in some of BCCI's deceptions in the United States; that beginning in late 1977 they assisted BCCI in purchasing Financial General Bankshares with the participation of nominees while understanding BCCI's central involvement in directing and controlling the transaction; and that they concealed BCCI's financing of their own First American shares from First American's other directors and from U.S. regulators.
facts.quote: Regardless of whether Clifford and Altman were deceived by BCCI in some respects, both men participated in some BCCI's deceptions in the United States.

facts.claim: On July 29, 1992, Clifford and Altman were indicted by a federal grand jury and by a New York State grand jury, the latter announced by Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau's office. The charges included conspiring to defraud the Federal Reserve Board by concealing BCCI's role in acquiring U.S. banks; the New York charges also alleged that they received millions of dollars in bribes from BCCI, and the federal case accused them of misleading regulators about BCCI's stake in First American. Both denied the charges; Clifford said he had been a victim of BCCI.
facts.quote: They were charged with conspiring to defraud the Federal Reserve Board by concealing BCCI's role in acquiring U.S. banks.

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) records that in July 1992 the Federal Reserve issued charges against Clifford and Altman proposing to bar them from banking for life, and states that Altman lied to the Federal Reserve in his sworn testimony about the sale of CCAH stock.
facts.quote: In July 1992 the Fed issued charges against Clifford and Altman, proposing to bar them from banking for life.

facts.claim: On August 14, 1993, after a five-month trial in which the court had dismissed the central bribery count for lack of evidence, a Manhattan State Supreme Court jury acquitted Robert Altman of the remaining charges in the New York BCCI bank-fraud case.
facts.quote: a Manhattan State Supreme Court jury finding Altman innocent on all four counts

sources.title: Jury acquits Altman in BCCI case

facts.claim: In November 1993, New York State Supreme Court Justice John Bradley dismissed the New York case against Clifford, on a motion requested by both District Attorney Morgenthau and Clifford's defense lawyer, on the ground that Clifford's age and health made him unable to stand trial.
facts.quote: Justice John Bradley dismissed the case against him in November 1993, on a motion requested by both Morgenthau and Clifford's defense lawyer.

sources.title: Charges dropped against Clark Clifford in BCCI case

facts.claim: On February 3, 1998, the Federal Reserve Board announced it had settled, with their consent, the administrative proceedings it had brought against Clark M. Clifford and Robert A. Altman in connection with the BCCI affair. Without admitting any of the Board's allegations, the two agreed to turn over most of their shares in the holding company, a transfer the Board valued at about $5 million, for the benefit of BCCI's depositors and creditors; Altman also agreed not to participate in the banking industry without the Board's prior approval. The Board dismissed its prohibition action against Clifford, citing his age and health.
facts.quote: Altman has also agreed not to participate in the banking industry without the prior approval of the Board.

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) records that Acting CIA Director Richard Kerr, testifying in October 1991, acknowledged what the Subcommittee had heard the previous day from former First American president Robert Altman: that the CIA had made extensive use of First American, the bank holding company Clifford chaired, for a variety of purposes, including ordinary banking and savings accounts. The report adds that the CIA later informed Subcommittee staff that neither Clifford nor Altman had been made aware of the existence of the accounts before the summer of 1991.
facts.quote: the CIA had made extensive use of First American for a variety of purposes, including for ordinary banking and savings accounts / neither Clifford nor Altman had been made aware of the existence of the accounts prior to the summer of 1991

openQuestions: The exact counts in the 1992 indictments differ between accounts (UPI describes four counts at the New York trial; Time describes eight felony charges at the start). The federal indictment's disposition after Altman's acquittal (reported as dismissed by the Justice Department) was not confirmed from a primary source.

Reports that Clifford made about $6 million in profit on First American stock bought with an unsecured BCCI loan appeared in search results (Time, 'A Capital Scandal', https://time.com/archive/6717182/a-capital-scandal/) but the passage's page was not confirmed; left out.

Web search budget ran out before the UPI 1993 and Deseret 1992 articles could be re-queried for verbatim passages; quotes for the indictment and dismissal facts are taken from search-result extracts and should be checked against the pages.

The Federal Reserve's July 29, 1991 release (https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/files/19910729.pdf) names BCCI, CCAH and individuals including Abedi and Naqvi; whether it names Clifford or Altman was not established, and the Fed's charges against the two are dated July 1992 by the Senate report. The February 3, 1998 settlement release is already cited; its PDF companion was listed by the first round.
